info.bio:
Patricia Mae Andrzejewski (Brooklyn, Nueva York, Estados Unidos; 10 de enero de 1953), conocida como Pat Benatar, es una cantante de Rock de Estados Unidos, quien tuvo numerosos éxitos durante la década de 1980s, tales como "Heartbreaker", "I Need A Lover", y "You Better Run", el segundo vídeo que fue transmitido en MTV tras el de The Buggles' Video Killed the Radio Star.

Patricia Mae Andrzejewski nacida de una familia Polaca-Irlandesa en Brooklyn, pero creció en Lindehurst, Nueva York, inicialmente estudió ópera como su madre.

scenes.name: Fundamentalismo, pánico satánico y acoso al metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El metal es el último blanco de una larga tradición conservadora contra la música popular: el jazz que «causó la perdición» de mil chicas de Chicago en 1921-22, el rock and roll que el Ku Klux Klan llamaba música salvaje de negros, el folk «comunista», el rock drogado de Spiro Agnew. A finales de los setenta la derecha fundamentalista resurge justo cuando el metal crece y MTV lo mete en las casas. Se queman discos (Iowa en 1980, Saint Paul en 1981, una escuela baptista de Florida en 1982 que destruye «Hell Is for Children» de Pat Benatar, una canción contra el maltrato infantil); se buscan mensajes satánicos grabados al revés (el «experto» Wilson Bryan Key los encontraba hasta en las galletas Ritz); psiquiatras como Paul King sacan conclusiones de pacientes ingresados en sus clínicas; la policía de California usa un manual que pide censurar Creem, Hit Parader y Circus; detienen en escena a Sebastian Bach, de Skid Row, por mover la pelvis; se cancela un concierto de Metallica en Notre Dame; los colegios prohíben camisetas y hay quien quiere «desmetalizar» a los fans. Para Weinstein el satanismo del metal no es una contrateología sino un juego dionisíaco con los símbolos, heredero del blues: si la sociedad pone el éxtasis en el lado del mal, el metal se llama a sí mismo malo.

podcast.title: "I Want My MTV" Campaign
podcast.body: Pat Benatar was one of the prominent artists who appeared in promos for the "I Want My MTV" campaign. This highly effective campaign encouraged people to call their local cable companies to demand that they carry the new channel, significantly expanding MTV's reach and power across the US. "Promos like this began to run constantly on MTV featuring the police, Pat Benatar, Pete Townsend, Cindy Loper, Billy Eidle, and even David Bowie."

podcast.title: Enduring Marriage and Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Induction
podcast.body: Pat Benatar married her band's guitarist, Neil Geraldo, in 1982; he was her second husband. The couple has remained together since their marriage and were jointly inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022. "He was her second husband and they married in 1982. They've been together ever since and in 2022, we're inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame together."

podcast.title: MTV Commercial Appearance
podcast.body: Pat Benatar appeared in an early MTV commercial, shouting the iconic phrase "I want my MTV!" alongside The Police and Pete Townshend. "By the way, that's the police shouting, I want my MTV! At the start of that TV commercial, just before Pat Benatar and Pete Townsend."

podcast.title: Reputation as Album Rock Leader
podcast.body: Pat Benatar spent years establishing herself as the "leading woman on album rock radio" before her 1984 crossover success with "Love is a Battlefield." This background highlighted her established rock credentials prior to experimenting with dance-oriented sounds. "She'd spent years building a reputation as the leading woman on album rock radio."

podcast.title: Rock Credibility and AOR Radio
podcast.body: Pat Benatar is presented as a "rocker gal" who established herself on Album-oriented Rock (AOR) radio before moving towards poppier songs. Crucially, unlike Madonna, Benatar "remained a fixture on rock radio" and successfully made Billboard's rock tracks charts, serving as a contrast to how female artists with dance-pop elements were treated by the rock format. "But unlike Madonna, who was never played by rock stations, Benatar remained a fixture on rock radio."
